Lessons.Title: The Correlation Coefficient
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: interpret the correlation coefficient r as a description of the direction and strength of a linear association in paired numerical data; distinguish perfect linear relationships, weak linear association, and undefined r. Independently authored Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 3 Lesson 7, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/3/7/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0). The source uses matching scatter plots with correlation descriptions rather than presenting a mechanical regression recipe alone.

First-party perfect positive dataset pairs (1,2),(2,4),(3,6),(4,8) lie exactly on y=2x, so r=+1. First-party perfect negative pairs (1,8),(2,6),(3,4),(4,2) lie on y=10−2x, so r=−1. Correlation sign indicates direction and |r| indicates strength of *linear* association, not rate, units or causality.

Original U-shaped dataset x=−2,−1,0,1,2 and y=4,1,0,1,4 has Pearson r=0 because symmetrical positive and negative x deviations cancel the covariance. A clear nonlinear relationship exists despite no linear correlation. A data set with all x values identical has no defined Pearson r because the x standard deviation is zero; do not grade r=0 for an undefined denominator.

Student matching task: label at least four scatter plots as perfect positive, perfect negative, nonlinear with near-zero r, or undefined r. Explain how shifting/rescaling positive units can leave r unchanged while a negative vertical multiplier reverses its sign. Discuss why r is descriptive, not proof of cause.

Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, maximum 8): accurate direction/strength assignment, evidence from point trends, correct handling of nonlinear/undefined cases, and critical interpretation with no causal overclaim. Human reasoning and actual plotted evidence matter.

KeyConcepts.Title: Pearson r
KeyConcepts.Definition: Unitless number between −1 and 1 describing direction and strength of linear relationship.
KeyConcepts.Rule: r=+1 for perfect positive line; r=−1 for perfect negative line.

KeyConcepts.Title: Linear versus nonlinear association
KeyConcepts.Definition: Correlation r measures linear pattern, not all kinds of dependence.
KeyConcepts.Rule: A curved relationship can have r=0.
KeyConcepts.Example: Symmetric U-shaped y=x² has zero sample Pearson correlation for symmetric x-values.

KeyConcepts.Title: Undefined correlation
KeyConcepts.Definition: Pearson r cannot be calculated if one variable has zero variance.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Do not substitute zero for division by zero.
KeyConcepts.Example: All x=3 make the x standard deviation zero and r undefined.

WorkedExamples.Title: Recognize a perfect positive line
WorkedExamples.Question: What is r for x=1,2,3,4 and y=2,4,6,8?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the exact first-party paired-data model, compute each quantity, and interpret mathematical evidence.
Steps: As x rises, y rises proportionally at a constant positive rate.
All points lie exactly on a nonvertical straight line.
Nonzero variance in both variables guarantees r=+1 for this perfect positive relation.
WorkedExamples.Check: The sign and perfect-line condition agree.

WorkedExamples.Title: Recognize a negative line
WorkedExamples.Question: What is r for x=1,2,3,4 and y=8,6,4,2?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the exact first-party paired-data model, compute each quantity, and interpret mathematical evidence.
Steps: As x rises by 1, y falls by exactly 2.
Both variables vary and points lie on a perfect decreasing line.
WorkedExamples.Check: Perfect negative direction with nonzero variances.

WorkedExamples.Title: Explain a zero linear correlation with curvature
WorkedExamples.Question: What can r say about x=−2,−1,0,1,2 and y=4,1,0,1,4?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the exact first-party paired-data model, compute each quantity, and interpret mathematical evidence.
Steps: Both x and y vary so the Pearson denominator is nonzero.
The covariance numerator is zero, hence r=0.
But y=x² is a deterministic U-shaped association, not independence.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Pearson r=0 though a nonlinear relationship is present.
WorkedExamples.Check: Symmetry cancels linear covariance but does not erase curvature.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: r is a standardized strength/direction measure with no units; slope has output/input units.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Separate rate of change from correlation.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Interpreting r=0 as no possible relationship
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A U-shaped deterministic relation can have zero linear correlation.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Examine the scatter pattern for nonlinearity.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Calling undefined r equal to zero
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A zero standard deviation makes the formula undefined.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Report undefined when all values of one variable are identical.

SummaryPoints: Pearson r lies between −1 and +1 and is unitless.
Perfect increasing and decreasing straight lines have r=+1 and −1 respectively.
r=0 does not rule out nonlinear association; zero-variance data leave r undefined.
Teacher-scored plot interpretation must not be replaced with unsupported causal claims.
